questions.question: Two million drivers are online and each sends one location update every four seconds. What peak update rate enters the location pipeline?
options: 125,000 updates/second
500,000 updates/second
2,000,000 updates/second
8,000,000 updates/second
questions.explanation: Divide concurrently online drivers by the update interval: 2,000,000 / 4 = 500,000 updates per second. Daily active drivers are not the same as concurrent drivers.

questions.question: Why should dispatch expand a geo-cell search ring by ring instead of querying an entire city at once?
options: It guarantees the globally optimal assignment
It bounds candidate work while allowing sparse areas to search farther
It makes GPS coordinates strongly consistent
It removes the need to calculate ETA
questions.explanation: Ring expansion keeps the first query local, stops after enough eligible candidates are found, and searches farther only when supply is sparse. Exact ETA scoring still follows.

questions.question: Which write most directly prevents one driver from accepting two active trips during a race?
options: A process-local mutex in one matcher
An eventually consistent cache overwrite
A durable conditional claim on driver availability and version
A larger notification queue
questions.explanation: A conditional claim makes one durable writer win. Local locks do not coordinate separate processes, and last-write-wins can overwrite an already promised assignment.

questions.question: A delayed location packet arrives after a newer packet. What should the hot location index use to avoid moving the driver backward in time?
options: Packet arrival order only
A driver-scoped sequence number or event timestamp plus a freshness lease
The rider's payment status
A global table scan
questions.explanation: A monotonic driver sequence or trusted event time rejects older updates, while a lease or TTL prevents disconnected drivers from remaining available forever.

questions.question: The payment provider times out after a trip completes. What is the safest retry design?
options: Create a new charge identity on every retry
Move the trip back to in-progress
Retry with the same trip-scoped idempotency key and reconcile the uncertain result
Block safety reporting until payment succeeds
questions.explanation: The trip remains completed while payment becomes a recoverable workflow. Reusing one idempotency key limits duplicate effects, and reconciliation resolves uncertain provider outcomes.

questions.question: Which partition key best preserves the order of one driver's location updates while still allowing parallel processing across drivers?
options: A random key for every update
The driver ID
One global city key
The current latitude string
questions.explanation: Using driver ID sends one driver's updates to the same partition, preserving that driver's sequence while different drivers can be processed in parallel.

questions.question: During a regional dispatch outage, which degraded behavior best protects correctness?
options: Allow two regions to assign the same driver
Keep showing stale drivers with no age bound
Stop new matches in affected cells while preserving active-trip state and safety reporting
Retry every dependency without admission control
questions.explanation: It is safer to reject or delay new matches than to violate assignment ownership. Active trips and the isolated safety path have higher continuity priority.

questions.question: Why should raw GPS history and authoritative trip state use different storage and retention policies?
options: They have identical consistency and audit needs
Location telemetry is high-volume and often short-lived, while trip and payment records require durable business history
Trip state never changes
GPS points must participate in payment transactions
questions.explanation: Hot location data optimizes recent proximity decisions and can be compacted or expired. Trip, fare, payment, and safety records have stronger correctness, audit, and recovery requirements.
